title: The brothers bow (Genesis 42)
hook: his brothers come for grain and don't recognize him; he turns away and weeps

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner who ended the day running Egypt. Your line was plan for the lean years. What did you set aside? Day three hundred seventy-one.

The good years come, and Joseph fills the storehouses. Then the famine arrives, just as the dreams said, and it reaches far beyond Egypt, all the way to Canaan, where an old man named Jacob is watching his family go hungry. He hears there's grain in Egypt. He tells his sons: why do you just sit there looking at one another? Go down and buy some. Ten brothers go. The youngest, Benjamin, Rachel's other son, stays home. Jacob has already lost one of Rachel's boys. He won't risk the second. So ten men walk into Egypt to stand in line for bread, in front of the governor of the land.
screen: `THE FAMINE REACHES CANAAN.` → `TEN BROTHERS GO DOWN.` → `BENJAMIN STAYS HOME.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Joseph's brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth." Years after the dream of the sheaves, here it is. The sheaves are bowing, and Joseph remembered the dreams, the text says. And: "Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him." Of course they don't. He was a teenager in a coat. Now he's a grown Egyptian official, shaved, speaking through an interpreter. He speaks roughly to them. He accuses them of being spies. He puts them in custody for three days. Then he lets them go, but keeps one brother, Simeon, bound, until they come back with the youngest. And the brothers, not knowing he understands every word, start talking to each other in their own language. "We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear." All these years later, the pit is still in the room. Then this: "And he turned himself about from them, and wept." The powerful governor steps away so no one sees his face, cries, and comes back to keep testing them. Why does he test them? Genesis doesn't say. Readers have wondered whether he wants to know if they've changed, or whether he's simply hurt and doesn't know what to do yet. Genesis leaves both open. Look at the week behind us: Esau running to his brother, the coat, the pit, Potiphar's house, the forgotten prisoner, the dreams by the Nile. Under all of it sits a family that broke. And now, in this chapter, the brothers say out loud what they did.
screen: `THE SHEAVES BOW AT LAST.` · `HE KNEW THEM; THEY KNEW NOT HIM.` · `WE ARE VERILY GUILTY.` · `THE GOVERNOR TURNS AWAY AND WEEPS.` · then, large: `AND HE TURNED HIMSELF ABOUT FROM THEM, AND WEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice tears you've hidden. Settle, and breathe. Maybe there was a time you turned away so no one would see you cry: at work, at a funeral, in the car before walking into the house. You don't have to cry now. Just notice what was being carried then, and how long it was carried alone. Then let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God. If you don't, simply be gentle with the person you were then. The bell holds the time.
The brothers bow. Ten brothers come to Egypt for grain and bow before the governor, not knowing he is Joseph, the brother they sold.
Your line: he turned away and wept. Today, if you see someone holding it together in public, give them a little room, and a little kindness. Day three hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Genesis 42 as a story about guilt surfacing years later, and preachers use the brothers' confession to talk about honesty and repentance within families.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. the brothers who sold you are bowing at your feet, and they don't know you. you understand every word they say to each other. what do you do?
options: tell them who you are at once.
speak roughly, test them, and turn away to weep.

fork.reveal: he accuses them of spying, keeps Simeon, and sends them for Benjamin. and when he hears them admit their guilt, he turns away and weeps.

original.note: Hebrew: to weep. Joseph weeps again and again in the chapters that follow.

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph gets his revenge on his brothers.
what it means: he tests them hard, but the scene turns on his tears, and the brothers' confession: we are verily guilty.
what a scholar hears: the brothers speak freely because Joseph uses an interpreter; the reader, like Joseph, hears what they think no one else understands.

notes: 'Twenty years after the dream': Joseph was 17 (37:2), 30 before Pharaoh (41:46), plus seven years of plenty and some famine; roughly twenty years. Confirm the round number.
Week-end look-back (days 365–370) folded into the end of the teach.
'He accuses them of being spies' (42:9) and Simeon bound (42:24). Confirm.
Joseph's weeping recurs (43:30; 45:2, 14–15; 46:29; 50:1, 17); the original note says 'again and again' rather than giving a count.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'twenty years' (voice, myth reveal, trapdoor), which Genesis 42 does not state, and tied the sheaves to 42:9 ('Joseph remembered the dreams'); 'in Hebrew' became 'in their own language'; look-back no longer claims every story is about a broken family; removed 'for the first time' and 'both feel true'; practice no longer tells the listener what they were or felt.
